note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — SMALL GREEN PANICLE, THEN ROOTED BASE
tiles.details: Follow ONE plant from its panicle to basal tillers. A small loose green panicle (Kew 1–12 cm; UT Austin local 7–9.5 cm) and hooded leaf tips suggest Poa, but P. arachnifera and lawn Poa share the tip. P. annua is usually annual and tufted, although some turf biotypes persist or root at nodes; absence of a visible rhizome in a landscape photograph proves nothing.
tiles.short: Low cool-season introduced bluegrass; open triangular panicles, soft folded blades and boat-prow tips are useful clues, not species proof.
tiles.status: FIELD CUE VISIBLE — CONNECTED LOCAL ROOTED BASE NEEDED

tiles.heading: 02 · TRUE MEMBRANOUS LIGULE / COLLAR
tiles.details: The true ligule is a tissue flap, NOT the folded boat tip or a white portion of the sheath. Kew GrassBase describes an eciliate membranous ligule 2–5 mm; existing Williamson County treatment gives approximately 0.5–3 mm. The source-authenticated Stefan.lefnaer four-view collar photograph includes a genuine 10-mm bar but does not prove a precise measurement on a Hays plant. Poa arachnifera also has a membranous ligule; inspect reproductive characters.
tiles.short: Open the INNER blade–sheath junction: a pale unfringed membrane, often ~2–5 mm in Kew's treatment; local descriptions may be shorter.
tiles.status: REAL SOURCE COLLAR PHOTO — SAME-PLANT 1-MM MEASUREMENT NEEDED

tiles.heading: 03 · MATURE SPIKELETS / FLOWERING SEX
tiles.details: Measure an intact mature spikelet, excluding the stalk, before dissection. Each laterally compressed spikelet bears two basal glumes and multiple florets. UT Austin describes lower/intermediate florets generally bisexual, with upper florets sometimes pistillate or vestigial; DO NOT teach that every floret is invariably bisexual. Texas bluegrass is dioecious (male and female plants separate). Existing Harry Rose spikelet photographs do not independently show sex or separate organ boundaries.
tiles.short: Many-flowered awnless spikelets: local Texas description ~3–5 mm with 2–6 florets; Kew's broader treatment ~3–10 mm and 3–10 fertile florets.
tiles.status: PUBLISHED SEX/MEASUREMENTS — LOCAL DISSECTION STILL NEEDED

tiles.heading: 04 · LOWER / UPPER GLUME MEASUREMENTS
tiles.details: UT Austin's Central Texas description gives lower 1.4–2 mm and upper 2–2.5 mm; Kew GrassBase gives lower 1.5–3 mm (1 vein) and upper 2–4 mm (3 veins). Separate BOTH persistent glumes at the spikelet base and photograph front/back with a 1-mm scale before drawing any vein or glume arrow. The photographed overlapping green scales do not resolve which is which.
tiles.short: Lower glume ~1.4–3 mm, usually 1-veined; upper ~2–4 mm, usually 3-veined (Texas/Kew treatment ranges).
tiles.status: PUBLISHED ANATOMY — MEASURED SEPARATED GLUMES NEEDED

tiles.heading: 05 · FERTILE LEMMA / PALEA / AWN AND LOOK-ALIKES
tiles.details: UT Austin gives the lowest lemma ~2.5–3.2 mm; Kew gives ~2.5–4 mm, five-veined and awnless. The palea sits inside the lemma, has two keels and may bear keel hairs. Compare native Texas bluegrass (P. arachnifera): connected perennial rhizomes and separate male/female flowering individuals; source-authenticated Harms female images show cobwebby basal lemma hairs, but this character must be viewed on real female florets. Introduced Kentucky bluegrass (P. pratensis) is also rhizomatous but has bisexual flowers; P. trivialis may be stoloniferous. Never use boat-tip, green color or web-like texture alone to name the species.
tiles.short: Fertile lemma ~2.5–4 mm, usually 5-veined, often hairy along veins; NO lemma awn.
tiles.status: SOURCE ANATOMY + LOOK-ALIKES — DISSECTION/SEX STILL UNPROVEN

tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE / PHOTO AND SITE QA HANDOFF
tiles.details: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO (Grass Photo-Finish): Hays-authenticated rooted flowering tuft and panicle on one plant; opened true inner ligule beside a 1-mm ruler; one attached mature spikelet at scale followed by separated lower/upper glumes (vein counts), awnless lemma, palea and visible bisexual lower floret; same-scale Poa annua versus P. arachnifera/P. pratensis comparison. NEEDS_SITE_QA (Public Learner Readiness): check all six archived records and five teaching panels, per-image CC BY 2.0/CC BY-SA 4.0 creator/source/rights, existing arrow endpoints, EXIF/GPS and mobile rendering. The archived Harry Rose spikelet6 JPEG has not been byte/pixel verified: do not create an anatomy panel or arrows until it passes. Do not mark FINISHED until identity, decisive anatomical photographs, publication rights, precise arrows and live page QA are confirmed.
tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS: six source-identified JPEGs and five teaching panels, plus critical local root-to-floret confirmation remaining.

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: ANNUAL BLUEGRASS — INTRODUCED, usually low cool-season annual. Recognize low soft green flowering tufts, often many small open triangular panicles and folded boat-prow leaf tips. The NEW macro really shows the boat tip, and the NEW four-view photo shows a membrane-like LIGULE at the blade/sheath junction. BOTH details are shared by other Poa: for species confirmation, document an intact rooted tuft (usually no persistent connected rhizomes) and a ripe spikelet of normally bisexual florets. The length of a photographed ligule or green head alone is NOT decisive.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: Find the small low flowering tuft and whole open green panicle; compare the existing Harry Rose field photo.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Follow ONE plant from its panicle to basal tillers. A small loose green panicle (Kew 1–12 cm; UT Austin local 7–9.5 cm) and hooded leaf tips suggest Poa, but P. arachnifera and lawn Poa share the tip. P. annua is usually annual and tufted, although some turf biotypes persist or root at nodes; absence of a visible rhizome in a landscape photograph proves nothing.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Follow ONE plant from its panicle to basal tillers. A small loose green panicle (Kew 1–12 cm; UT Austin local 7–9.5 cm) and hooded leaf tips suggest Poa, but P. arachnifera and lawn Poa share the tip. P. annua is usually annual and tufted, although some turf biotypes persist or root at nodes; absence of a visible rhizome in a landscape photograph proves nothing.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Contrast native P. arachnifera: perennial connected RHIZOMES and separate male/female flowering individuals; a pistillate female's ripe lemma bases produce dense long cobwebby hair tufts, while P. annua flowers generally bisexual and may have keel/marginal hairs but lacks the massive female web character. Do not guess sex or exact lemma hairs from landscape photos; compare P. pratensis and P. trivialis separately where common lawn grasses overlap.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.caption: Whole plant photo shows low flowering grass, green leaves, and flowering branches. Neither microscopic lemma characters nor ligule is resolvable.

panels.label: ANNUAL BLUEGRASS — boat-prow shaped leaf tip
panels.caption: The green blade narrows to a blunt folded, keel-like 'prow' tip. The lightened very tip is visible; it may be a worn or dry margin, not a separate auricle. The photographer reported magnification 30×, but supplied no calibrated ruler. This proves the shared Poa leaf tip shape, not annual versus Texas bluegrass.
panels.creator: Jason Hollinger
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: ANNUAL BLUEGRASS — actual membranous ligule and blade/sheath collar
panels.caption: Four source-photo views show the same kind of grass blade/sheath collar. The bottom view exposes the whitish membranous flap (ligule) exactly where green blade separates from the upper sheath. The genuine 10-mm photo scale sits at bottom; do not confuse the entire pale sheath with the ligule or infer its precise size without local measurement.
panels.creator: Stefan.lefnaer
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: ANNUAL BLUEGRASS — source-identified spikelet with upper-floret palea
panels.caption: Harry Rose's source-identified P. annua close-up shows green overlapping spikelet scales, a visibly pink-tinged tip, and the flowering branch. Three arrows mark only these clearly visible structures. His original caption identifies a palea in an upper floret, but this crop does not independently resolve which scale is the palea versus glume or lemma. No millimeter scale or proof of bisexuality is visible.

panels.label: ANNUAL BLUEGRASS — ACTUAL EXPOSED FIBROUS ROOTS AND LEAFY CROWN
panels.caption: Source-identified Poa annua pulled aside at a stone edge, revealing long white fibrous roots connected to a green leafy crown. This is a Danish vegetative plant, not a Hays County flowering voucher. No visible root system alone proves a complete absence of rhizomes.

panels.label: ANNUAL BLUEGRASS — REAL DANGLING YELLOW ANTHERS ON A SPIKELET
panels.caption: An actual photographed spikelet: small yellow anthers protrude at left, beside overlapping green and pale pointed floret scales. Source is an Australian specimen (Harry Rose), not a Hays County specimen. The roughly 5-mm spikelet size comes from the photographer's description and is not measured by a ruler in this image.

intro: ANNUAL BLUEGRASS — INTRODUCED, usually low cool-season annual. Recognize low soft green flowering tufts, often many small open triangular panicles and folded boat-prow leaf tips. The NEW macro really shows the boat tip, and the NEW four-view photo shows a membrane-like LIGULE at the blade/sheath junction. memory_rule: BOAT TIP + LIGULE = POA GENUS. P. ANNUA = usually annual and bisexual; P. ARACHNIFERA = perennial rhizomes and separate SEXES with WEBBY female lemma bases.
safety_note: Photographed 30× leaf tip and 4-view ligule images belong to P. annua sources, not Texas bluegrass. Texas female webby lemma hairs and connected rhizomes are unphotographed.
field_rule: Document same-plant base and reproductive sex; do not identify species from boat-shaped leaf apex alone.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
